questions.stem: What does Corporate Data refer to?
options: All the information that belongs to a company and is used to run its business
Only the financial accounts of a company
Only the data stored in the IT department's servers
Public information about a company's share price
questions.explanation: Corporate data is the complete collection of information that belongs to a company and helps it function and grow, created by employees, systems, customers and partners.

questions.stem: Which category of corporate data includes day-to-day transactions such as sales orders, payments and inventory updates?
questions.explanation: Operational data covers day-to-day transactions such as sales orders, payments and inventory updates.

questions.stem: Which category of corporate data includes core entities such as customers, products, employees and suppliers?
questions.explanation: Master data includes the core entities of the business: customers, products, employees and suppliers.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of unstructured corporate data?
options: A database table of sales orders
Call recordings and social media comments
questions.explanation: Unstructured data includes emails, PDFs, contracts, social media comments and call recordings.

questions.stem: Which category of corporate data includes aggregated and historical information used for reporting and decision-making?
questions.explanation: Analytical data is aggregated and historical information used for reporting and decision-making.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed as a department in which corporate data exists?
questions.explanation: Corporate data exists across finance, sales, marketing, operations, HR, supply chain, customer service and IT; astronomy is not among them.

questions.stem: What can poor-quality or poorly governed corporate data lead to?
options: Wrong strategies, financial losses or regulatory risks
questions.explanation: Poor-quality or poorly governed data can lead to wrong strategies, financial losses or regulatory risks, which is why organisations invest in governance and quality management.

questions.stem: Although HR manages employee records and finance manages accounting systems, who owns corporate data?
options: Each department owns its data exclusively
The IT department owns all data
The organisation as a whole, since corporate data is a strategic asset
The individual employee who created it
questions.explanation: Although departments manage their own data, corporate data belongs to the organisation as a whole and is considered a strategic asset.

questions.stem: In the school example of corporate data, why can the principal's question 'How many students improved their Maths scores this year?' only be answered from properly stored and managed data?
options: Because the principal is not allowed to ask teachers
Because only the IT department knows the answer
Because if the data is incomplete or incorrect, the answers will also be wrong
Because Maths scores are unstructured data
questions.explanation: Just as companies rely on corporate data to answer business questions, if the school's data is incomplete or incorrect the answers will also be wrong.

questions.stem: What is the key idea about corporate data?
options: It is simply stored information with no strategic value
It should be kept only by the finance team
It is a risk that should be minimised by storing less
It matters only for daily operations, not long-term planning
When managed properly it becomes a competitive advantage; when ignored it becomes a risk
questions.explanation: Corporate data is a valuable resource supporting operations, planning and growth; managed properly it is a competitive advantage, ignored it becomes a risk.
